summary: A November 2015 Christian Science Monitor article by Beatrice Gitau reports a study of fish fossils from about 350 million years ago, arguing that the Hangenberg mass extinction removed large species and left smaller ones to dominate. Lauren Sallan of the University of Pennsylvania says smaller, faster-breeding fish gained an advantage, and that large animals may not be replaced for a very long time. The article also reviews theories of body size change, including Cope's rule and the Lilliput Effect, and notes that conservation efforts may still prevent a sixth mass extinction. Much of the page is Monitor boilerplate, navigation, subscription prompts and a letter from editor Mark Sappenfield, which were ignored.
one_line: A 2015 Monitor article reporting that after the Hangenberg mass extinction, small fish thrived while large species were slow to return.
key_facts: The article was written by Beatrice Gitau and published November 14, 2015.
The study analyzed fish that lived about 350 million years ago.
Researchers concluded that the Hangenberg event caused large species to die off while smaller species survived.
Lauren Sallan is an environmental scientist at the University of Pennsylvania.
Sallan said the result could be an ocean in which the rest of the fish are about the size of a sardine.
Sallan said the end result is an ocean in which most sharks are less than a meter (three feet) and most fishes and tetrapods are less than 10 centimeters, or smaller than a grapefruit.
Sallan's findings suggest smaller fish had an advantage because they breed much faster than their larger counterparts.
Cope's rule holds that a species tends to enlarge over time to avoid predation and become better hunters.
The Lilliput Effect holds that after mass extinctions there will inevitably be a temporary trend toward small body size, named after a fictional island in Gulliver's Travels.
Many scientists believe that we are on the brink of, if not in the midst of, a sixth mass extinction.
A summer report indicated that humans are chiefly to blame for the mass extinction already underway.
Humpback whales were recently recommended for removal from the endangered species list.
The research team, including scientists from Stanford, Princeton, and Berkeley, said rapid, intensified conservation efforts are needed to stave off a true mass extinction.

Sallan said disturbances are shifting natural selection so smaller, faster-reproducing fish are more likely to keep going, and it could take a really long time to get bigger fish back in any sizable way.
